name: Thyroid/hypothyroid evaluation

lead: People with persistent facial puffiness, especially around the eyes, get their thyroid checked, because hypothyroidism is a recognized medical cause of a puffy face. If it is found, treatment can reduce the puffiness along with other signs of the condition.

Low thyroid hormone can cause fluid-like buildup in the skin (myxedema). Clinical sources list a puffy face, dry coarse skin, hair loss and loss of the outer eyebrows among the signs. A TSH blood test is the usual first step. Many cases have few symptoms, and facial puffiness has other causes too.

paras: It starts with a visit to a clinician and a blood test, usually TSH. If low thyroid function is confirmed, a clinician prescribes treatment and monitors it with follow-up tests.
Treatment is prescription levothyroxine, with dose monitored by TSH, so diagnosis and treatment belong to clinicians. Self-treating with thyroid hormone is not advised.

angle.text: Testing thyroid hormone levels can reveal hypothyroidism, a recognized medical cause of a puffy face, especially around the eyes. If it is found, clinician-directed treatment can reduce the puffiness. It is a clinical workup rather than a cosmetic method.

lead: Thyroid evaluation is the blood-test workup for thyroid disorders, above all hypothyroidism, a condition in which the thyroid gland makes too little thyroid hormone. People interested in their appearance look into it because the condition can show up in the face and hair: a puffy face, especially around the eyes, pale and expressionless features, dry coarse skin, thinning hair and loss of the outer part of the eyebrows are all listed among its signs [1][2]. When a medical cause is behind persistent puffiness or hair changes, identifying it is the route to looking the way one otherwise would.

The usual first step is a TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) blood test, often repeated several weeks later, followed by free T4 if TSH is high. Standard treatment is the synthetic hormone levothyroxine, with doses adjusted by follow-up TSH results [1]. The opposite condition, hyperthyroidism, also has appearance-related signs, including weight loss, fine brittle hair and, in Graves' disease, bulging eyes and retracted eyelids [3][4]. Both conditions are common, and many people have mild or no symptoms, so testing is how they are confirmed or ruled out.

In looksmaxxing communities thyroid health comes up in threads on face puffiness, hair, eye area, height, jaw and body composition, where members swap lab results and discuss thyroid hormone, diet and supplements, often drawing on the writings of Ray Peat, who emphasised thyroid hormone in his account of metabolism [5][6][7]. Clinical guidance on diagnosis and treatment comes from bodies such as NICE, the American Thyroid Association and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists, as summarised in Wikipedia [1].

paras: Myxedema, the term for the skin and tissue changes of hypothyroidism, can produce an expressionless face, puffiness around the eyes and pallor. The swelling is described as non-pitting boggy edema, caused by the build-up of glycosaminoglycans in the dermis, and is most noticeable around the eyes, hands, feet and above the collarbones [2]. Hypothyroid skin is typically dry and coarse, with cool extremities, and the tongue can enlarge [1].

Many symptoms of hypothyroidism are common in people with normal thyroid function, and many people have mild symptoms or none. In middle-aged women the symptoms can be mistaken for those of menopause [1].

Hair loss is a listed sign of hypothyroidism, including loss of the outer third of the eyebrows, known as the sign of Hertoghe [1]. Hyperthyroidism is likewise associated with fine, brittle hair and hair loss [3]. Hashimoto thyroiditis, the commonest autoimmune cause of hypothyroidism, lists hair loss and dry skin among its symptoms [8].

Graves' ophthalmopathy, also called thyroid eye disease, is an autoimmune inflammation of the orbit that most often accompanies Graves' disease but can occur with Hashimoto thyroiditis or normal thyroid function. Upper eyelid retraction is its most common sign, giving a wide-open stare, and proptosis (bulging), swelling and redness can also occur [4]. About 20 to 25% of people with Graves' hyperthyroidism have clinically apparent eye involvement and 3 to 5% develop severe disease; smoking is associated with a roughly 7.7-fold higher incidence [4].

Treatment for appearance-relevant eye changes includes eyelid surgery, the most common procedure, and orbital decompression for proptosis, usually delayed until the disease has been stable for about six months. Teprotumumab was FDA-approved for the condition in January 2020 [4].

Weight gain with poor appetite is another listed symptom of hypothyroidism, which is why thyroid status is also discussed in body-composition threads on T Nation, where some posters describe a hypothyroidism diagnosis alongside difficulty controlling weight [1][9]. Hyperthyroidism more often brings weight loss despite good appetite [3].

A TSH test is the first-line screen. An elevated TSH indicates the gland is not producing enough hormone, a second TSH is usually checked several weeks later, and free T4 is then often measured. Overt hypothyroidism shows high TSH with low T4, while subclinical hypothyroidism shows raised TSH with normal free T4; central hypothyroidism shows normal or low TSH with low T4 [1]. AACE and NICE discourage routine T3 measurement when assessing for hypothyroidism [1]. Reference ranges vary by assay and laboratory, so results are read against the range of the lab that ran the test [10].

Hashimoto thyroiditis is diagnosed with TSH, T4 and thyroid antibodies plus ultrasound; about 90% of patients have raised anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies, while some are seronegative [8]. Hashimoto usually begins between ages 30 and 50 and affects women roughly 8 to 15 times as often as men [8].

Iodine deficiency is the most common cause worldwide, with about a billion people estimated to be iodine-deficient, and Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause where iodine intake is sufficient. Less common causes include prior radioactive iodine or thyroid surgery, medications such as lithium and amiodarone, and pituitary or hypothalamic problems (central hypothyroidism) [1]. Women are about seven times as likely as men to have a TSH above 10 mU/L, and the condition is more common after age 60 [1].

Hypothyroidism is managed with levothyroxine (synthetic T4), with TSH checked 4 to 8 weeks after starting or changing the dose and again at 6 and 12 months once stable [1]. Food and calcium can reduce absorption, so it is usually taken apart from meals [1]. Thyroid medication is described as safe in pregnancy [1]. Dietary iodine adequacy matters, and the same source notes that too much iodine may worsen some forms of the condition [1].

Liothyronine (T3) alone is not well studied, and adding it to T4 has not been confirmed to improve symptoms. The British Thyroid Association (2007) reported more side effects and no added benefit, the European Thyroid Association (2012) allows a three-month experimental trial, the American Thyroid Association (2014) recommends against routine use and NICE discourages it. Desiccated animal thyroid, containing T4, T3 and other compounds, has been largely abandoned since the 1970s and is discouraged by British, American and NICE guidelines [1].

For subclinical hypothyroidism, NICE advises treating when TSH exceeds 10 mIU/L and considering a time-limited trial for symptomatic people with lower values, whereas American guidelines allow treatment for symptoms, positive anti-TPO antibodies or heart-disease risk; Wikipedia notes there is no demonstrated benefit in non-pregnant people and some risk of overtreatment [1]. Overtreatment with thyroid hormone is associated with the signs of hyperthyroidism [3].

The condition now called myxedema was recognised in the 1870s and linked to thyroid removal in the 1880s. In 1891 George Redmayne Murray treated a 46-year-old woman with injected sheep thyroid extract; she improved within weeks and lived another 28 years on the treatment [1][2]. Purified thyroxine followed in 1914, synthetic thyroxine in the 1930s and liothyronine was identified in 1952 [1]. Hakaru Hashimoto described the autoimmune thyroiditis that bears his name in 1912, and studies in 1956 established it as autoimmune [8]. The TSH radioimmunoassay arrived in 1971, after which many patients treated on older tests were found to have excess hormone [1].

No studies have examined thyroid testing specifically as a strategy for facial appearance. Studies of thyroid conditions themselves include several that relate to nutrition. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials examined selenium supplementation in Hashimoto thyroiditis, with TSH, thyroid antibodies and ultrasound findings among its outcomes [11]. A randomised trial in Hashimoto patients looked at selenium's effect on thyroid autoimmunity and regulatory T cells [12]. A double-blind randomised trial tested ashwagandha root extract in people with subclinical hypothyroidism [13], and another randomised trial examined myo-inositol combined with selenium in Hashimoto patients with subclinical hypothyroidism [14].

A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the relationship between iron deficiency and thyroid function [15], and a 2024 review summarised the role of nutrition in thyroid function [16]. For thyroid eye disease, the evidence base is described by Wikipedia as including corticosteroids, teprotumumab, and mixed or limited evidence for radiotherapy, selenium in mild disease and tocilizumab [4].

On looksmax.org the thyroid appears in several kinds of thread: long posts linking energy metabolism and facial structure, drawing on Ray Peat's idea that energy and structure are interdependent [5]; posts on mental health and Hashimoto's [6]; lab-result threads in which members ask Peat-influenced peers to interpret their results [7]; and threads comparing desiccated and synthetic thyroid [17], asking how to use T3 and T4 for heightmaxxing [18], and asking whether a thyroid condition affects side-profile appearance [19]. Another thread is titled 'the thyroid mog is the most brutal' [20].

On T Nation, posters mention hypothyroidism mainly in connection with weight control, fatigue and body composition, and one thread discusses self-medicating with T3 [9][21]. Clinical guidance notes that adding T3 to levothyroxine has not been confirmed to improve symptoms [1].
